summary: Phase 1 — Engine Foundation
description: Implement exponential decay and session priming. Ship minimal visualization (decay brightness + priming rings). Goal: validate the core loop end-to-end with the cheapest mechanisms first.

summary: Phase 2 — Memory Integrity
description: Implement synaptic tagging & consolidation. Add consolidation ring visualization. Add contradiction/tension edge type. Goal: fix decay's blind spot for long-term-important notes before building further on top of it.

summary: Phase 3 — Retrieval Upgrade
description: Implement spreading activation. Add live pulse animation + activation path trace. Add Live/Study speed toggle. Goal: the actual retrieval quality upgrade — the mechanism most directly improving Claude Code context assembly.

summary: Phase 4 — Structural Signals
description: Implement PageRank-style hub importance and community detection. Add hub sizing and cluster coloring. Goal: structural/visualization polish — the D3 plugin phase already planned.

summary: Phase 5 — MCP Retrieval Reliability
description: Implement guaranteed minimum-k with threshold relaxation, tiered fallback chain (incl. keyword fallback), per-call timeout budget, and retrieval logging/observability. Goal: the MCP tool that Claude Code calls never returns empty-handed, and failures are visible before they cause a bad session.

summary: Phase 6 — Case Study Packaging
description: Build the "why was this retrieved" ablation/diff view. Record Live vs Study demo captures for presentation. Write up each mechanism against its cognitive-science source as the case-study narrative. Goal: package the working system as a product demo and research-grounded case study.

summary: As the engine, I decay edge/node strength exponentially so recency reflects the Ebbinghaus forgetting curve
description: strength(t) = strength_0 \* e^(-t/τ), τ tunable per note-type. Live computation at query time using last_accessed + base_strength, not a scheduled batch job.

description: decayWeight() already exists and is correct (packages/core/src/decay.ts), but it's only applied during compact() batches (packages/core/src/compactor.ts) -- i.e. once per compaction run, not per query. getWeightedNeighbors (packages/core/src/query.ts) currently reads the already-compacted weight straight from link-weights.json with no further decay applied for time elapsed since the last compaction. This ticket wires decayWeight(record.weight, daysSince(record.lastTouched)) into the read path so ranking reflects continuous decay, not just decay-as-of-last-compaction.

summary: As Claude Code, I get a priming boost for notes related to the current session so context stays coherent
description: In-memory LRU buffer of last N accessed notes per session. retrieval_score(note) = base_score + priming_bonus(note, session_buffer). No persistence, session-scoped only.

parentSummary: As Claude Code, I get a priming boost for notes related to the current session so context stays coherent
summary: Build LRU session buffer + priming_bonus scoring function
description: No session-scoped state exists today -- get_weighted_neighbors and search_notes (packages/mcp-server/src/tools.ts) are stateless per call. Add an in-memory LRU buffer (last N accessed notes) scoped to the MCP server instance/session, and a priming_bonus(note, buffer) function blended into retrieval_score. Session-only, no persistence or decay math needed -- matches the doc's framing as the lightest lift of the six mechanisms.

summary: As a user, I see node brightness reflect decay and a warm ring around primed notes in the graph view
description: Minimal visualization layer validating Phase 1 mechanisms visually: node/edge brightness = freshness; dashed warm ring = session-buffer membership.

summary: As the engine, I promote edges to a consolidated tier after repeated reactivation so important notes don't get lost to decay
description: Two-tier weight: recent_score (fast decay, updates on co-access) and consolidated_score (promoted via nightly batch job once recent_score crosses threshold N times across M days). Models sleep-dependent memory consolidation.

parentSummary: As the engine, I promote edges to a consolidated tier after repeated reactivation so important notes don't get lost to decay

description: EdgeRecord (packages/core/src/types.ts) currently has a single weight field; split into recent_score (fast decay, reusing existing decayWeight logic) and consolidated_score (promoted after crossing a threshold N times across M days). Note: no scheduler exists anywhere in the repo today -- compaction currently only runs on-demand via the compact_weights MCP tool or the vnl-compact.js bin. This ticket also needs to stand up the first actual scheduled/nightly job, not just the promotion logic -- treat that as real new infrastructure, not a config change.

summary: As a user, I see a gold ring on notes that have been consolidated into long-term memory
description: Visual proof the two-tier system works: consolidated nodes get a persistent gold border, distinct from merely-recent fading nodes.

summary: As the engine, I support a "supersedes/conflicts with" edge type so outdated notes surface their successor
description: Distinct edge type beyond positive association, flagging tension/contradiction (e.g. old ADR vs. its revision). Retrieval surfaces "this note may be outdated — see its successor" even when the old note is still fresh by recency.

summary: As the engine, I spread activation across bounded multi-hop neighbors so indirect context surfaces on query
description: activate(node, energy) recursively transfers energy_edge_weight_decay_per_hop to neighbors, bounded at 2-3 hops, cutoff at min_threshold. Replaces direct-neighbor-only retrieval in Claude Code context assembly.

parentSummary: As the engine, I spread activation across bounded multi-hop neighbors so indirect context surfaces on query
summary: Implement bounded recursive activation traversal + threshold cutoff
description: getWeightedNeighbors (packages/core/src/query.ts) today only returns direct neighbors (single hop) sorted by weight -- there is no multi-hop traversal anywhere in the codebase yet. Replace with activate(node, energy=1.0) recursion per the doc's formula: transferred = energy \* edge_weight \* decay_per_hop, bounded to 2-3 hops, cutoff at min_threshold. This is the core architectural change of Phase 3 and the first true graph-traversal logic in the engine.

summary: As a user, I watch activation pulse hop-by-hop through the graph with a visible retrieval path trace
description: WebSocket event stream (node_activated, edge_traversed) from engine to D3 plugin. Side panel logs actual retrieval path (e.g. "M+S Hydraulic → SAP Sales Cloud → \[2 hops\] → Discovery Phase template") so the mechanism is auditable, not decorative.

summary: As a user, I can switch between Live and Study playback speed for the activation animation
description: Two-state switch: Live (real ms-scale timing) vs Study (staggered \~150-300ms per hop). Applied only at the rendering layer — engine timing itself is never altered, same as slow-motion footage of a real event.

summary: As the engine, I compute PageRank-style importance so hub notes stay weighted even when not recently touched
description: importance(node) = (1-d) + d \* Σ(importance(neighbor)/out_degree(neighbor)). Computed periodically (batch, not per-query). Blended into retrieval: final_score = activation_score \* (1 + λ \* importance).

summary: As the engine, I run Louvain/Leiden clustering so topic communities are auto-discovered without manual tagging
description: Periodic clustering job assigns cluster_id per node. Feeds the visualization layer (node color) rather than retrieval directly. Sequencing note: only build after weighting system (Phases 1-3) is mature, since cluster quality depends on edge-weight quality.

summary: As a user, I see node size reflect hub importance and node color reflect cluster in the D3 visualization
description: Node size scales with PageRank score. Node color = cluster assignment from community detection. This is the originally-planned D3 visualization plugin phase.

summary: As Claude Code, I always receive at least k results from an MCP query, even under sparse activation
description: Guaranteed minimum-k (e.g. k=3): progressively relax activation min_threshold rather than returning an empty set when spreading activation + priming produce fewer than k qualifying nodes.

summary: As Claude Code, I never get an empty MCP response — a tiered fallback chain always serves something
description: Fallback order: (1) full spreading activation, (2) relaxed-threshold activation, (3) structural-link floor weight — a precomputed bidirectional wikilink adjacency graph (built during compact()/vnl-nightly.js, persisted like link-weights.json) contributes neighbors at a configurable floor weight (default 0.1) for pairs with no existing usage-weighted edge, so real usage always outranks structural-only presence; shared by getWeightedNeighbors and activate via computeLiveNeighborWeights, (4) plain keyword/substring match over titles+tags, (5) most-recently-consolidated notes as last resort. Response indicates which tier served the result. Tier 3 specifically rescues cold-start/sparse-cluster notes with no usage history yet but real wikilink structure (e.g. bunit2/AML/InvoiceFlow domains observed 2026-07-14 to have zero weighted edges despite active recent work — real links exist, just never traversed/reinforced via MCP calls).

summary: As an operator, I have a bounded per-call timeout and full retrieval logging so failures are visible before they cause a bad session
description: Hard time budget per MCP call (e.g. 300ms) returning partial results instead of blocking. Log every call: query, tier served, result count, latency — to catch a whole cluster systematically falling through to fallback before a client demo.

summary: As a reviewer, I can toggle layers on/off and see a "why was this retrieved" ablation diff
description: Before/after panel showing what context would look like without a given layer (e.g. "activation only" vs "activation + priming") — turns the demo into a genuine ablation study, the strongest scientific-credibility asset for the case study.

summary: As Brain Space, I have recorded demo captures and a written case study mapping each mechanism to its science source
description: Record Live vs Study demo captures for presentation. Write up each mechanism (decay, consolidation, activation, priming, hubs, clusters) against its cognitive-science source as the case-study narrative for product positioning.

summary: Phase 7 — Science Research & Validation
description: Ongoing literature review to validate existing mechanisms and identify new cognitive-science candidates for the engine. Each addition must answer: does this make the system better at picking the right notes out of thousands, or is it decoration? Goal: keep the science layer rigorous and defensible for the case study, not just aesthetically neuroscience-flavored.

summary: As the research lead, I compile a literature review validating each mechanism and screening new candidates
description: Deep-dive literature review of each shipped mechanism's grounding (Ebbinghaus, Frey & Morris, Collins & Loftus, priming studies, PageRank, Louvain/Leiden) plus one round of adjacent candidates: emotional salience/arousal effects on memory strength, context-dependent memory (state-dependent recall), interference theory (proactive/retroactive), chunking, dual-coding.

summary: As the research lead, I run ablation evaluations measuring retrieval quality per mechanism
description: Design and run a controlled evaluation comparing retrieval quality (precision of "right 5 notes out of 5,000") with each mechanism on vs. off, individually and combined. This is the empirical backbone the case study needs — turns "we think this helps" into a measured result.

description: Generalize the engine beyond Obsidian: split into a pluggable source-adapter layer (Obsidian vault, Notion, Confluence, Azure Wiki, plain folder of docs) feeding a generic node/edge graph, keeping the engine/MCP/reliability layers (Phases 1-5) untouched underneath. Deliberately parked as its own initiative, separate framing from the personal-PKM pitch — same engine, different audience (enterprise knowledge base vs. personal tool).

summary: As an architect, I define a pluggable source-adapter interface so the engine is source-agnostic
description: Define a common interface: parse X into nodes+edges. Obsidian adapter (wikilinks) is the reference implementation. Everything below this line (engine, MCP, reliability) stays untouched regardless of source.

summary: As the engine, I infer candidate edges via AI when a source has no explicit links (Confluence, Azure Wiki, Word docs)
description: For sources without explicit wikilinks (Confluence, Azure Wiki, plain Word docs): entity/topic co-occurrence for candidate edges, an LLM pass judging "does A reference/depend on/supersede B?", confidence-weighted edges that start weak and earn full weight only through consolidation (reusing Phase 2 machinery). Usage co-access remains the ground-truth validator, unchanged from the Obsidian version.

summary: As the engine, I apply per-note-type decay live at query time instead of baking it in at compaction
description:
Edge weights now store `baseStrength` (undecayed, raw accumulated weight from events) instead of a pre-decayed `weight`. Decay is computed live at query time via `liveWeight()`, using a configurable half-life per note frontmatter `type` (`resolveHalfLifeDays` / `NoteTypeDecayConfig` — moc: 90d, atomic: 30d, project: 14d, default: 30d).

Implemented in:

* `packages/core/src/decay.ts` — `resolveHalfLifeDays`
* `packages/core/src/types.ts` — `EdgeRecord.baseStrength`, `NoteTypeDecayConfig`
* `packages/core/src/query.ts` — `liveWeight()` used by `getWeightedNeighbors` / `getEdgeWeight`
* `packages/obsidian-plugin/src/view/ForceSim.ts` — inlined equivalent live-decay formula for the graph view (browser bundle can't import core's Node-only runtime, only its types)
* `packages/core/src/compactor.ts` — updated to stop pre-decaying weight at compaction

Shipped in commit 529f10c ("decay and phase 1") but was not tracked as a Jira issue before implementation. Filing retroactively to keep AIBRAIN-1 status accurate.

summary: compactWeightsTool test call sites fail tsc --noEmit: handler takes 0 args, tests pass ({})
description:
`packages/mcp-server/src/tools.ts` — `compactWeightsTool.handler` is `(ctx: ToolContext) => async () => {...}` (zero params). `packages/mcp-server/test/tools.test.ts` calls it as `compactWeightsTool.handler(ctx)({})` at 8 call sites (lines 51, 66, 77, 102, 117, 132, 143, 170), passing an unwanted argument.

`npx tsc --noEmit -p packages/mcp-server` fails with 8x `TS2554: Expected 0 arguments, but got 1.`

Confirmed pre-existing on `main` at commit d0026a3, independent of any in-flight work — verified via `git stash` + fresh `core` dist rebuild + `tsc --noEmit`, error persists with zero local changes present. vitest doesn't catch it because it only transpiles (strips types) rather than type-checking, so the test suite reports green while `tsc --noEmit` fails. `tsup` build also doesn't catch it since it only compiles `src`, not `test`.

Fix is either: give `compactWeightsTool`'s handler an (unused/optional) parameter to match the other tools' handler shape, or drop the `({})` argument at each test call site. Low severity — doesn't block runtime or the build, but breaks a clean `tsc --noEmit` gate and should be fixed before CI treats that as a requirement.

summary: Graph view UI/UX pass: brain icon, dismissible retrieval panel, interim clustering layout
description:
User-reported UI/UX issues with the Obsidian plugin's Neural Graph view, fixed in commit f96f04f:

1. Graph looked like an unstructured hairball compared to Obsidian's native graph view.
2. Retrieval path panel had no way to hide/dismiss it — stayed open permanently.
3. Ribbon/tab icon was the default "git-fork" Lucide icon, not on-brand.

Fixes:

* Ribbon icon and view tab icon switched to "brain" (main.ts, NeuralGraphView.ts).
* RetrievalPathPanel.ts + styles.css: added a collapse toggle in the panel header.
* ForceSim.ts: added a lightweight deterministic label-propagation clustering pass (new Clustering.ts) that pulls detected communities toward distinct anchor points, as a stopgap ahead of the real Louvain/Leiden work tracked in AIBRAIN-22. Tuned charge/link/collide physics and the isolate-ring force (previously sized off a single max-distance outlier, now off a percentile with a symmetric band) so unlinked notes settle into one tight ring instead of scattering.
* Renderer.ts: reduced edge opacity/thickness to read closer to Obsidian's native graph's minimal-ink style.

Note: Clustering.ts's label-propagation approach is intentionally throwaway — AIBRAIN-22 should replace it with real Louvain/Leiden modularity optimization, at which point the anchor-pulling force in ForceSim.ts can just consume its cluster assignments instead.

summary: Radial star layout: importance pulls nodes toward each cluster's own center
description:
Clusters were already spatially separated into regions (cluster-anchor force, AIBRAIN-22/23) and colored by community (hue ordering, AIBRAIN-23 follow-up), but within a region all nodes were pulled toward the anchor with equal strength — no radial organization by importance, so hub notes didn't visually stand out within their own cluster.

Added a second radial component to `createClusterForce` (packages/obsidian-plugin/src/view/ForceSim.ts): each node's target distance from its cluster's anchor is now `INTRA_CLUSTER_MAX_RADIUS * (1 - importance)`, using the existing min-max normalized PageRank score (note-importance.json, AIBRAIN-21). High-importance nodes settle near the region's own center, low-importance nodes toward its rim — each cluster now reads as its own small star instead of a flat blob.

Depends on the nightly job having populated note-importance.json at least once (setGraphMetadata) — before that all nodes have importance 0 and sit uniformly at the rim.

summary: Shared core-backed read path for SessionStart MOC/Inbox context
description:
The global hard rule says all vault .md interaction goes through vault-neural-link MCP tools, enforced by \~/.claude/hooks/enforce-vault-mcp.ps1 (a PreToolUse hook denying native Read/Edit/Write/MultiEdit under the vault). But \~/.claude/hooks/vault-session-start.ps1 (the SessionStart hook that dumps MOCs/_.md into context every session) reads those files with raw Get-ChildItem/Get-Content, completely outside that gate — SessionStart fires before any tool call exists for a PreToolUse hook to intercept, and hooks are shell subprocesses that can't invoke mcp__vault-neural-link_\__ tools directly. This has been a silent loophole since the hook was written.

Fix: give the hook and the MCP server one shared read path in packages/core instead of the hook re-implementing its own file walk.

1. Add packages/core/src/sessionContext.ts: getMocSections(vaultPath), getInboxFlag(vaultPath), buildSessionStartContext(vaultPath) — reusing the existing listNotes pattern from packages/core/src/notes.ts, raw file reads (not parsed NoteRef) to preserve the current verbatim dump format. Export from packages/core/src/index.ts.
2. Add packages/core/bin/vnl-session-context.js (same shape as the existing vnl-compact.js/vnl-nightly.js bin scripts): imports from ../dist/index.js, takes vaultPath as argv\[2\], must fail open (never exit non-zero, print nothing on error) since a broken context-loader must never block session start. Prints the complete SessionStart hook JSON payload to stdout. Add "vnl-session-context" to packages/core/package.json's bin field.
3. Rewrite \~/.claude/hooks/vault-session-start.ps1 to resolve CLAUDE_VAULT_PATH then just shell out to `node <repo>/packages/core/bin/vnl-session-context.js $vaultFull` and pass stdout through — removing all direct Get-ChildItem/Get-Content vault access from the hook. Repo path hardcoded the same way \~/.claude.json already hardcodes the MCP server's dist path (existing convention, not new fragility) — note this should switch to resolving via the installed package once AIBRAIN-40..44 (npm publish) lands.
4. Update the "Harness tool routing (hard rules)" section of the global \~/.claude/CLAUDE.md to document SessionStart context-loading as a stated exception (read-only, pre-agent-turn, now backed by the same packages/core code the MCP server uses) — same treatment as the existing .yml/.yaml exception, turning a silent gap into a deliberate documented one.

Full plan captured in the vault — see linked note.

summary: As Obsidian, I own the daily compact/consolidation cycle myself, with no external scheduler or Claude Code trigger
description:
Move the daily weight-compaction pipeline (`compact` -> `runNightlyConsolidation` -> `rebuildStructuralIndex` -> `runImportanceComputation` -> `runClusterComputation`, currently `packages/core/bin/vnl-nightly.js`) into the Obsidian plugin itself, so it self-schedules from inside `packages/obsidian-plugin` while Obsidian is open.

Remove the two external triggers this replaces:

* Windows Scheduled Task (`INSTALL.md` step 7, `schtasks /create ... vnl-compact.js ...`)
* Any reliance on a Claude Code session to kick off compaction (`compact_weights` MCP tool as the effective trigger, `.claude/settings.local.json` cron-adjacent Bash permission for `node bin/vnl-compact.js`)

Hard requirement: **100% idempotency, exactly one full run per calendar day, triggered only by Obsidian itself.**

Key risk already identified: `runNightlyConsolidation` (`packages/core/src/consolidation.ts`) has NO internal same-day guard today — the code comment states it must only be invoked by a real once-a-day cron, or repeated same-day calls double-promote edges past the reactivation threshold. A plugin-side scheduler must add an explicit last-run-date gate (persisted via plugin `loadData()`/`saveData()`, not just an in-memory interval) before calling it, checked on every plugin load and on a periodic in-session timer, so:

* reopening Obsidian multiple times in one day never re-runs consolidation
* leaving Obsidian open across a midnight rollover still triggers exactly one run for the new day
* the plugin surviving a crash/reload mid-run doesn't produce a partial or duplicate day marker

Also update `INSTALL.md` (drop step 7 entirely) and `docs/spec.md` bin/cron references to reflect the plugin as the sole scheduler; CLI (`vnl-compact.js`/`vnl-nightly.js`) can remain as a manual/headless fallback but is no longer the primary path.

summary: Retrieval Benchmark vs. Baselines + Personal Usage Analytics
description:
Before validating monetization (AIBRAIN-49/59/60/61), answer a more fundamental question: does the Hebbian/decay/activation engine actually beat free, naive alternatives, and how does the user's own usage look in practice?

AIBRAIN-31's ablation harness (`packages/core/scripts/eval-retrieval.mjs`) already measures which of the engine's own layers carry the most weight (structuralFallback > priming > importance > consolidation, per its results note) — but it only compares the engine against itself with layers toggled off. It never compares against an external baseline: plain grep/full-text search, embedding-based semantic search, or a naive full-context-stuffing (CAG-style) approach. Without that comparison there's no evidence the system's complexity earns its keep over a $0 alternative.

Separately, the plugin already logs every session's traversal/reinforce/search events to append-only JSONL (`.vault-neural-links/events/`), but nothing summarizes that data back to the user as "how do I actually use this, what happens when I do." That's a personal-usage report, distinct from AIBRAIN-60's install/conversion funnel analytics for the paid-tier decision.

Goal: this epic sits ahead of AIBRAIN-61's decision gate, not parallel to it — proving real advantage over free alternatives is a precondition for "will anyone pay," not just a nice-to-have.

1. Plain full-text/filename grep search (zero intelligence baseline)
2. Embedding-based semantic search over note content (no graph, no weights, no decay — a minimal RAG)
3. Optional: naive full-context-stuffing (CAG-style: dump all/most notes into context) if corpus size allows a fair test

Measure the same precision/rank metrics already used in AIBRAIN-31's results against each baseline. This answers the question AIBRAIN-31 didn't: not "which of our layers matters most" but "does the whole system beat a $0 alternative, and by how much."

summary: Deterministic usage instrumentation — stop delegating logging decisions to the LLM
description:
The MCP server currently relies on Claude (the calling agent) to _notice_ certain events and _decide_, mid-conversation, to call a tool reporting them — `reinforce_link` ("use this when a link materially helped"), `log_traversal`'s manual-credit path, and implicitly `search_notes` (nobody decided it should persist at all). This is a judgment-triggered logging pattern, not a deterministic one, and it fails silently: per AIBRAIN-68's usage report, `reinforce_link` has zero recorded invocations across the entire logged history despite months of real traversal activity.

This epic replaces judgment-triggered logging with outcome-triggered logging the server owns unconditionally, ahead of and independent from the Phase 4 standalone-decoupling decision (AIBRAIN-61/AIBRAIN-50) — it improves the data quality that decision itself depends on (ablation results, importance scoring, usage reports all consume this same event log).

Full audit of all 12 MCP tools, current decision-owner per tool, and the proposed fix is documented in the vault: see \[\[MCP Tool Decision-Delegation Audit and Deterministic Logging Plan\]\] (VaultNeuralLinks domain).

Not in scope here: folding `activate`/`get_weighted_neighbors` into an owned context-assembly pipeline, and moving `ablation_diff`/`get_edge_weight`/`compact_weights` off the agent-facing tool list — those require the actual standalone backend and are tracked as acceptance detail on AIBRAIN-62 instead, since they're gated by AIBRAIN-61.

summary: Persist every search_notes call to the event log
description:
`search_notes` currently only calls `client.touch()` (in-memory session priming) — it never calls `appendEvent`/`appendRetrievalLog`, so there is no persisted trace of search activity anywhere on disk. This isn't a judgment gap like `reinforce_link`, just an omission: nobody wired search into the existing append-only logger that `traverse`/`reinforce` already use.

Fix: add a `search` entry to the `EventType` union (or a parallel lightweight log) and have `searchNotesTool`'s handler unconditionally append one per call — query, result count, whether weighting was used — regardless of what the caller does with the results.

Acceptance: `computeUsageReport()` (AIBRAIN-68) can report real search counts instead of the "can't be measured" caveat in its `gaps` field; that caveat is removed once this ships.

parentSummary: Deterministic usage instrumentation — stop delegating logging decisions to the LLM
summary: Replace reinforce_link's LLM-judgment trigger with outcome-based auto-reinforcement
description:
`reinforce_link` asks Claude to notice, mid-conversation, that a link "materially helped" and call a tool about it. Per AIBRAIN-68's usage report this has never actually fired — zero recorded invocations across the whole logged history — so the deeper-engagement signal the weighting model was designed to have never exists in practice; all persisted weight currently comes from passive `read_note` traversal only.

Fix: deprecate the manual trigger in favor of a deterministic, server-computed signal derived from actual conversation outcome:

1. After a response is generated, check which notes were in the assembled context (from `activate`/`get_weighted_neighbors`/`search_notes` results) AND were actually cited/quoted in the final answer text — auto-apply the reinforcement boost to those edges, no LLM call required.
2. Optionally layer an explicit user-facing signal (a 👍 on an answer, or equivalent) as a stronger deterministic boost on top — a UI event, not a tool call an agent might skip.

Keep `reinforce_link` as a callable tool during the transition (some clients may still want explicit control) but stop treating it as the primary mechanism, and update its tool description to reflect that it's now a manual override on top of automatic reinforcement rather than the only path.

Acceptance: reinforce events start appearing in `events/*.jsonl` from real sessions without requiring any explicit tool call; `computeUsageReport()`'s "reinforce_link was never called" gap stops firing once there's real automatic reinforcement history.

Parent epic: AIBRAIN-69.

parentSummary: Deterministic usage instrumentation — stop delegating logging decisions to the LLM
summary: Remove log_traversal's manual-credit path once auto-logging covers its gap
description:
`log_traversal`'s manual path exists only to patch a gap in `read_note`'s automatic traversal logging ("reach for it only when an edge should be credited without both notes having gone through read_note"). That's the same shape of problem as `reinforce_link` — closing a gap by asking the LLM to notice it exists — just lower-impact since auto-logging already covers most cases.

Fix: identify what actually causes the gap (e.g. content already known without a `read_note` call, or a hop that skipped a read) and close it with a deterministic server-side hook tied to whatever event represents "this note actually entered context" — not a manual tool call. Once closed, remove the manual-credit path from the tool surface (or fold it into the same automatic mechanism as AIBRAIN-70/reinforce work) rather than leaving a rarely-used escape hatch that depends on the agent remembering it exists.

Depends on / do alongside: the auto-reinforcement story (AIBRAIN-69's other story) — both replace an agent-judgment trigger with an event-driven one, so should share the same underlying "note entered context" hook if practical.

Parent epic: AIBRAIN-69.

summary: Licensing/subscription backend — Stripe direct integration, paid from launch
description:
Product decision (2026-08-16, see vault \[\[Paid-From-Launch Monetization and Licensing Backend Decision\]\]): the plugin is paid from launch, not freemium. Obsidian's community store has no built-in payment processing — the plugin installs free from Browse and must gate its actual functionality behind an entitlement check against infrastructure we own. This makes a licensing/subscription backend launch-blocking, not a follow-up.

Decisions locked in:

* No marketplace resellers (Gumroad/Lemon Squeezy ruled out — they act as Merchant of Record and put their brand between us and the customer).
* Direct Stripe integration. We are the Merchant of Record (chosen over Paddle knowingly — lower fees, but we personally own VAT/sales-tax registration and remittance obligations once relevant thresholds are crossed).

Scope:

* Stripe Checkout/Billing for subscription capture + recurring billing.
* Owned backend receiving Stripe webhooks (checkout.session.completed, customer.subscription.updated, invoice.payment_failed, etc.) and maintaining its own entitlement/license database.
* License verification endpoint the plugin calls to check whether a given license is currently active.
* Plugin-side: settings UI for entering/checking a license key, and graceful degradation when unlicensed/expired.
* Same backend should also host the previously-decided opt-in, self-hosted telemetry mechanism (AIBRAIN-60) — one service, two concerns — rather than standing up separate infrastructure.

Explicitly NOT in scope here: the legal/tax assessment itself (entity structure, ToS, privacy policy, VAT/sales-tax registration under Stripe-as-MoR) — that's the user's own review and blocks real transactions going live, independent of this engineering work.

Depends on / should be sequenced with: AIBRAIN-39 (packaging/distribution — the plugin still needs the npm/bundling fixes regardless of paid-vs-free).

summary: Scale testing: synthetic 300k-note corpus + performance benchmarking
description:
The real vault has \~250 notes. Nothing has been tested at anywhere near the scale a real customer's vault could reach (300k notes was used as the target order of magnitude). Extends the existing baseline benchmark work (packages/core/scripts/benchmark-baselines.mjs, from the AIBRAIN-68 usage-report commit) rather than starting fresh.

Mock data approach: real large interlinked-note corpora essentially don't exist publicly at this scale for this shape of data, so the primary source is a synthetic generator — but a naive uniform-random link generator would under-stress the system, since real note graphs (like Wikipedia's) exhibit power-law/small-world structure (a few heavily-linked hub notes, many sparsely-linked leaves). Use a preferential-attachment (Barabasi-Albert style) topology generator instead of uniform random, so hub-heavy structural stress (PageRank, clustering, spreading activation) is actually exercised.

Stories:

* Synthetic vault generator: parameterized by note count, avg links/note, cluster count, using preferential-attachment topology; extends benchmark-baselines.mjs
* Wikipedia-derived real-world link-graph sample as a secondary, more "real" validation corpus (freely available dumps/pagelinks data) — cross-check that synthetic generation isn't accidentally easier or harder than real-world topology
* Run the full pipeline (parse, structural index build, compaction/decay, PageRank, Louvain clustering, nightly pipeline) at 300k scale; capture timing/memory numbers against defined acceptance thresholds
* Document bottlenecks/scaling limits found — this is a discovery story, not a pre-committed fix; decide follow-up perf work only after seeing real numbers

Related: AIBRAIN-31 (existing internal ablation harness this extends conceptually), AIBRAIN-66/67/68 (retrieval benchmark + usage analytics epic this scale work supports).

summary: OKF format support: implementation + scale/mock-data validation
description:
Google published the Open Knowledge Format (OKF) 2026-06-12 as v0.1 (Apache 2.0, GitHub) — a small, deliberately minimal spec: markdown files with a small YAML frontmatter block, one concept per file, only "type" required in v0.1 (title/description/resource/tags/timestamp optional). Positioned as the format for giving AI agents curated context, not a finished standard yet ("a starting point").

The detailed implementation plan already exists in the vault — see \[\[OKF Link Migration Plan\]\] (5 phases: extract shared target-resolution helper, dual-syntax link parsing in core, switch auto-generated links to OKF syntax, Obsidian vault setting, migrate existing notes) — saved 2026-07-20, not yet executed. This epic executes that plan AND adds the scale/mock-data validation the user specifically asked for, since OKF is 2 months old and no large real-world OKF corpus exists yet to test against — synthetic generation is the only real option right now.

Stories:

* Re-validate the existing migration plan's assumptions against the actual published OKF v0.1 spec doc directly (the plan was drafted the same window OKF was announced — confirm frontmatter field assumptions, link-syntax assumptions match the real spec rather than an early impression of it)
* Execute Phases A-C of the migration plan (shared resolver extraction, dual-syntax parsing in core, auto-generated links switch to OKF syntax) — implementation
* Execute Phase D (Obsidian vault setting + manual verification) and Phase E (migrate this vault's existing \~250 notes, dry-run first)
* Synthetic large-scale OKF corpus generator: reuse the topology generator from the 300k-note scale-testing epic but emit OKF-shaped files (YAML frontmatter with type/title/description/resource/tags/timestamp per spec, relative markdown links) instead of wikilink-style notes
* Run the engine against the synthetic OKF corpus at scale (aligned with the 300k target); validate parsing/adapter correctness AND performance, not just correctness at small scale

Related: AIBRAIN-34 (AI-inferred edges for non-wikilink sources — different problem, OKF already has explicit links so doesn't need inference), the scale-testing epic (shared topology generator).

summary: Anonymous, offline-first telemetry pipeline
description:
Implements the telemetry mechanism already decided (vault: "Telemetry Approach and Distribution Sequencing Decision" — opt-in only, self-hosted endpoint, no third-party analytics) now that AIBRAIN-73 gives it a real backend to land on. Refines that decision with three concrete requirements:

1. Anonymous — no PII, no note content/titles/paths in any event payload, identified only by an anonymous per-install token (not tied to a license/email/account).
2. Offline-first — the plugin works fully offline (per the product's existing offline-usability requirement), so telemetry must never block on network. Events queue locally and sync opportunistically.
3. Secured — both the local queue (at rest) and the sync transport (in transit) need real protection, not an afterthought, since it's still a stream of usage data even if anonymous.

Stories:

* Anonymous local event buffer: append-only local queue, anonymous per-install ID, no vault content in payloads
* Local storage security: restrict/protect the local telemetry queue file so it isn't a plaintext liability sitting on disk
* Offline-first batched sync: upload buffered events when online, retry/backoff, max-age/size eviction so an offline user doesn't accumulate unbounded local data
* Backend telemetry ingestion endpoint (extends AIBRAIN-73's backend): authenticated via the anonymous install token, rate-limited, TLS-only
* Opt-in first-run UX + settings toggle (must respect the existing opt-in-only decision, not silently default to on)
* Data minimization / anonymization spec: define the exact event schema up front and confirm nothing identifying can leak into it; feeds AIBRAIN-77's privacy policy disclosure text

Depends on AIBRAIN-73 (needs the backend to exist) and transitively AIBRAIN-78 (hosting). Relates to AIBRAIN-77 (privacy policy must disclose this) and AIBRAIN-60 (this epic is the concrete implementation of AIBRAIN-60's telemetry mechanism — AIBRAIN-60 itself stays as the broader install/WAU/conversion tracking goal, already flagged for re-scoping since there's no free tier to convert from anymore).

summary: Anonymous local event buffer
description: Append-only local queue for telemetry events, keyed by an anonymous per-install token generated on first run (not tied to license key, email, or account). Payload schema must never include note titles, paths, or content — structural/usage metrics only (e.g. tool-call counts, session duration, feature flags used).

summary: Local telemetry queue storage security
description: The local event buffer file needs real protection, not an afterthought — restrict filesystem permissions to the current user, avoid storing it somewhere auto-synced/backed-up unexpectedly, and treat it as a liability if it leaks even though the data is anonymous (usage patterns can still be sensitive).

summary: Offline-first batched sync with retry/backoff and eviction
description: Telemetry must never block plugin usage on network availability, consistent with the product's offline-usability requirement. Upload buffered events in batches when online; exponential backoff on failure; a max-age/max-size eviction policy so a long-offline user doesn't accumulate unbounded local queue growth.

summary: Backend telemetry ingestion endpoint
description: Extends AIBRAIN-73's backend. Accepts batched anonymous events, authenticated via the anonymous per-install token (not a license key), rate-limited per AIBRAIN-78's abuse-protection story, TLS-only transport.

summary: Opt-in first-run UX + settings toggle
description: Must respect the existing opt-in-only decision (vault: "Telemetry Approach and Distribution Sequencing Decision") — asks on first run, does not default to on, and stays visibly toggleable in settings afterward. No events are queued (not just "not sent") before the user opts in.

summary: Data minimization / anonymization spec
description: Define the exact event schema up front (field-by-field) and confirm nothing identifying can leak into it before any collection code is written. Output feeds directly into AIBRAIN-77's Privacy Policy story and the Obsidian README network-use disclosure.

summary: Persist get_weighted_neighbors() calls to the retrieval log
description:
activate() already persists every call to retrieval/{instance}.jsonl via appendRetrievalLog (AIBRAIN-26, index.ts:178), tested in index.test.ts. get_weighted_neighbors()'s client method (index.ts:153-156) only calls touch() for session priming — no persistence at all, so its call volume is invisible to computeUsageReport() and to any operator inspecting the retrieval log.

Fix (same shape as AIBRAIN-70 — deterministic, unconditional server-owned logging, not Claude-discretionary):

* Extend RetrievalLogEntry (types.ts) with a `source: "activate" | "get_weighted_neighbors"` field; make tier/relaxations/timedOut optional (activation-fallback-specific, don't apply to a direct neighbor lookup); add topK.
* Add the missing appendRetrievalLog call inside getWeightedNeighbors' client method.
* Tag activate's existing appendRetrievalLog call with source: "activate" for consistency.
* Update computeUsageReport() to aggregate/report both sources rather than assuming every retrieval-log entry is an activate() call.
* Tests: mirror index.test.ts's existing "logs every retrieveWithFallback call to retrieval-log.jsonl" case for getWeightedNeighbors.

Does not require the standalone backend or AIBRAIN-61 gate — small, same-day fix, distinct from AIBRAIN-62's larger "fold activate/get_weighted_neighbors into an owned context-assembly pipeline" scope.

summary: Obsidian plugin reads the desktop app's shared account session instead of its own license-key login
description:
Read half of the cross-app auth hand-off started in AIBRAIN-64 (commit 77f5fc0, `packages/core/src/accountSession.ts`). Per the 2026-08-18 architecture decision (vault note "Standalone Decoupled Product Direction - Open Question"), the Electron desktop app is the single auth/subscription surface — the plugin should not prompt its own independent login when the user reached it via the desktop app's "existing Obsidian vault" companion screen.

Write half already exists: `accountSessionPath()` (`~/.vault-neural-links/account-session.json`, fixed OS-level location, independent of any vault folder) + `readAccountSession`/`writeAccountSession`/`clearAccountSession` in `packages/core` — already `require()`'d unmodified by the plugin, so no new dependency needed. Desktop app's `auth:login`/`auth:logout` IPC handlers write/clear this file today.

Scope for this story:

* On plugin load, check `readAccountSession(accountSessionPath())` before falling back to the plugin's own license-key flow.
* Decide entitlement semantics here too — reuse the offline-grace-period design already drafted in vault note "Desktop App Login and Subscription Validation" (14-day grace, `lastValidatedAt`) rather than inventing a second scheme.
* The plugin's own standalone license-key login must stay working unchanged for the pre-existing plugin-only channel (someone who never installs the desktop app / no account-session file present).
* Not in scope here: plugin-connection-status detection surfaced back to the desktop app's companion screen — that's the reverse direction, separate work, still undesigned.

Depends on AIBRAIN-73 for the real verification endpoint eventually, but can be built/tested now against the desktop app's existing mock validator, same swap-seam approach `SubscriptionValidator` already uses.

summary: No entitlement gate exists: unauthorized users get full retrieval access today
description:
Confirmed gap, not yet fixed — user asked directly "what happens with the MCP server if not authorized" during AIBRAIN-64 OAuth work (2026-08-18). Checked both real surfaces:

* `packages/mcp-server` (the actual published npm package — the Obsidian channel people install today) has **zero auth code**. Grepped for any auth/entitlement/token/license reference — none exists. Anyone who registers it via `claude mcp add` with `CLAUDE_VAULT_PATH` set gets full `search_notes`/`activate`/`get_weighted_neighbors`/etc. access, free, no account, no check, today, in the shipped package.
* Desktop app's own `engine:search`/`engine:activate` IPC handlers (`packages/desktop-app/src/main.ts`) are also unguarded — the login/setup screens gate reaching the app UI, but nothing re-checks entitlement on each retrieval call; an expired access token mid-session doesn't stop search/activate from working.

This predates and is not fixed by AIBRAIN-64's OAuth work (commit 329b2fe) — that work makes a valid access token _available_ (via `packages/core`'s `accountSession.ts` cross-app hand-off), it doesn't make anything _check_ it.

Intended design (already scoped, not built — see vault note "Desktop App Login and Subscription Validation", item 3): gate `engine:search`/`engine:activate` **hard-block, not degrade** — no partial/degraded retrieval results when unauthorized, just an error directing the client to log in. The same gate needs to apply to the future bundled MCP server (AIBRAIN-62 territory) once it exists, and ideally to `packages/mcp-server` itself for the existing Obsidian channel — that package currently has no concept of authorization at all, which is the larger and more urgent gap since it's the one actually shipped and installable today.

Not scoped in this ticket: the actual verification logic against AIBRAIN-73's real backend (doesn't exist yet) — this should use the same token-expiry check available today (mock), swapped later.

summary: Investigate stale/noisy accumulated usage weight degrading rank-1 vs. zero-usage baseline
description:
benchmark-reinforcement.mjs (re-run 2026-08-28) shows the live vault's real accumulated usage weight (`asIs`, link-weights.json as it exists today) scores _worse_ on rank-1 than a zeroed-out usage tier (`zeroUsage`, pure structure+priming+importance):

* asIs: 16/18 found, 9/18 rank-1, mean rank 3.06
* zeroUsage: 16/18 found, 15/18 rank-1, mean rank 2.375
* simulatedReinforcement (fresh, realistic single retrieval-then-read event injected on top of zeroUsage): 18/18 found, 18/18 rank-1, mean rank 1.0

This is the opposite of what the usage/reinforcement tier is meant to do — real historical baseStrength is currently dragging rank quality down, while a single fresh, realistic usage event fixes it completely. Points at the specific accumulated weights being stale/noisy rather than the mechanism being wrong in principle.

Open question, not yet root-caused: is this decay miscalibration, or accumulated weight from now-irrelevant old traversals never getting pruned?

Full numbers and both benchmark re-runs (2026-08-23 and 2026-08-28) are in the vault: Notes/VaultNeuralLinks/AIBRAIN-67 Baseline Benchmark Results (## Updates, 2026-08-28 entry).

parentSummary: Scale testing: synthetic 300k-note corpus + performance benchmarking
summary: Desktop app note-list/graph render hangs at 300k-note scale — capped to top-N by importance
description:
Discovered live: with the desktop app's workspace pointed at sample-okf-large (300,003 OKF notes, the AIBRAIN-108 scale corpus), the login flow appeared to hang on "Waiting for browser…" for several minutes even though the browser-side OAuth exchange had already completed. Root cause wasn't auth — it was `loadAndShowFolder` in `packages/desktop-app/src/renderer.ts` auto-reopening the last workspace on login and then:

1. Building one `<li>` DOM element per note synchronously (300,000 of them).
2. Handing all 300,000 notes+edges to `ForceSim`/`Renderer` (render-core's force-directed physics simulation), which isn't built for anywhere near that node count.

The main process got saturated enough that it also delayed unrelated pending work (including the login IPC handler settling), which is why it looked like an auth bug from the outside. Electron eventually crashed under the load.

Note this is separate from AIBRAIN-118's `listNodes`/structural-index fix, which already handles the 300k case fine on the indexing side (confirmed in `main.ts`'s `workspace:load-folder` handler comment) — this bug was purely in what the desktop app _renders_.

**Fix implemented** (`packages/desktop-app/src/main.ts`, `renderer.ts`, `renderer/index.html`): `summarize()` now caps what's returned for the note list + graph to the top 500 notes by PageRank importance (`computePageRank`, the same score the radial-star graph layout already uses elsewhere) whenever a folder has more than 500 notes. Total counts are preserved (`noteCount` vs new `renderedNoteCount`), edges are filtered to only those between two rendered notes, and the UI shows "Showing top N of M notes by importance" when capped. `search`/`activate` are unaffected — they query the full on-disk structural index directly, not this summary.

Verified against the real sample-okf-large corpus (not a synthetic unit test): total load time \~31s (17s indexing + 14s PageRank-for-ranking), note list and graph both render correctly capped to 500 nodes instead of hanging/crashing.

**Known follow-up, deliberately deferred (user's call):** the 14s PageRank-for-capping cost is paid on every folder load. Could be cut by reading the nightly pipeline's already-persisted `note-importance.json` (`loadNoteImportance`) first and only falling back to a live `computePageRank` when no cache exists yet — at the cost of the ranking being up to a day stale. Not implemented this session; flagged here if it becomes a real annoyance in practice.

summary: searchNotes crashes (EMFILE/OOM) on broad queries against large vaults — unbounded concurrent weight lookups
description:
Discovered live while testing the AIBRAIN-131 desktop-app loading-screen UX against `sample-okf-large` (300,003-note OKF corpus): a search triggered on app launch (auto-resumed workspace) crashed the whole Electron process.

**Root cause**: `searchNotes` (`packages/core/src/notes.ts`) ran `Promise.all(hits.map(hit => getWeightedNeighbors(...)))` with no cap on `hits.length`. A broad query against a 300k-note vault produced \~8,000+ textual hits, so \~8,000 `getWeightedNeighbors` calls fired concurrently. Each one independently calls `loadWeights`/`loadNoteImportance`/`loadStructuralIndex`, and none of those are cached — every call is a fresh `readFile` + `JSON.parse` of disk state (including the large `structural-links.json` for a 300k-note vault). Thousands of concurrent file opens exceeded the OS file-descriptor limit (`EMFILE`), and holding that many parsed copies of a large JSON file in memory at once exhausted the V8 heap (`OOM`, process crashed).

Only `topK` (default 10) hits are ever returned, so scoring every textual hit by weight was pure waste on top of being the crash trigger.

**Fix implemented** (`packages/core/src/notes.ts`): capped the weight-scoring step to the first `WEIGHT_SCORE_CAP` (500) hits, processed in bounded batches of `WEIGHT_SCORE_CONCURRENCY` (25) rather than one unbounded `Promise.all`. Verified: `tsc --noEmit` clean, core rebuilt (`tsup`), desktop-app relaunched against `sample-okf-large` without crashing on startup search.

**Deliberately not done in this pass** (flagging as follow-up, same "good enough for now" call as AIBRAIN-131's deferred PageRank-cache optimization): `loadWeights`/`loadNoteImportance`/`loadStructuralIndex` are still re-read from disk once per scored hit (up to 500 times per search) instead of being loaded once and shared across the batch — the cap+batching fixes the crash and bounds the cost, but doesn't eliminate the redundant reads. Worth revisiting if search latency against large vaults becomes a real complaint.

Related: \[\[Desktop App Render Cap at Scale - Top-N by Importance\]\] (AIBRAIN-131) — same root class of bug (an operation that was fine at small-vault scale, unbounded against the 300k-note fixture), same test fixture that surfaced it.

summary: searchNotes has no content index — full-vault linear scan takes 130s+ at 300k-note scale
description:
Discovered live in the same session as AIBRAIN-132 (the EMFILE/OOM crash fix), testing the desktop app's search against `sample-okf-large` (300,003 OKF notes).

**The gap**: `searchNotes` (`packages/core/src/notes.ts`) has no persisted index over note bodies — only note titles/aliases get a cheap check, everything else requires a full `readNote` (file read + frontmatter parse) per candidate, for every note in the vault, on every single search call. There is no caching or incremental indexing of content at all.

**Measured** (`packages/desktop-app/scripts/repro-search.mjs`, real fixture, not synthetic):

* Fully sequential (pre-AIBRAIN-132 fix): the app hard-hung / never returned in a reasonable time (this is what looked like "nothing happens" when reported).
* Bounded concurrency 50 (AIBRAIN-132's stopgap): 203.8s.
* Bounded concurrency 250 (bumped once more this session): 129.5s.

The sublinear improvement (5x concurrency → only \~1.6x faster) shows the bottleneck is total disk/CPU work — reading and parsing every note body — not the concurrency level. Tuning the concurrency constant further has diminishing returns and risks reintroducing EMFILE at very high values (see AIBRAIN-132).

**What's actually needed**: a persisted content index (e.g. an inverted token index over note bodies, built/maintained incrementally like the existing structural-links/link-weights/note-importance indexes) so search doesn't need to re-read the entire vault on every query. Search would then look up candidates from the index and only read the handful of matched notes for snippet/context — same shape improvement as AIBRAIN-118 gave `listNodes()`.

**Not in scope for this ticket**: designing the index format/update strategy — that's the first task once this epic is picked up. `packages/core/src/notes.ts`'s current `CONTENT_SCAN_CONCURRENCY = 250` stopgap stays in place until this lands.

**Current stopgap status**: search against a 300k-note vault is slow (\~2 minutes) but no longer crashes or silently hangs — the desktop app now shows a "Searching…" indicator on the search button while it runs (this session's other fix), so it reads as working, just slow, rather than broken.

Related: AIBRAIN-132 (the crash fix in the same function), AIBRAIN-118 (the equivalent fix already done for `listNodes()`), AIBRAIN-108 (300k-scale testing epic that keeps surfacing this class of bug).

parentSummary: Retrieval Benchmark vs. Baselines + Personal Usage Analytics
summary: Define evidence-state taxonomy (Retrieved/Read/Re-query/Referenced/Helpful); don't feed raw telemetry into graph weights until correlation is measured
description:
Problem: our benchmark data (AIBRAIN-67, 2026-08-28 run) shows the live vault's real accumulated usage weight currently makes rank quality _worse_ than a clean slate (zeroUsage 15/18 rank-1 vs asIs 9/18) — i.e. we've already been feeding a behavioral signal into the ranking formula whose actual correlation with usefulness was never measured first. Don't repeat that mistake with the new telemetry work.

Define and document five explicit evidence states, and what the server can/can't actually know for each:

| State | Server can know? | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Retrieved | Yes | Returned by memory search |
| Read | Yes | Agent subsequently requested/read it |
| Re-query | Yes | Agent searched again after retrieval (weak negative signal) |
| Referenced | No, not MCP-only (needs UI human confirmation or the AIBRAIN-62 gateway) | Source appears to have contributed to final answer |
| Helpful | Only via feedback/strong attribution | Evidence that context actually helped |

Deliverable: a short reference note (vault + code comment on the scoring module) naming these states so future work doesn't silently slide from "we observed the agent read it" into "we know the agent used it." Then, once AIBRAIN-133/Memory Trace/feedback data (AIBRAIN-48 stories) exists, measure actual correlation between each behavioral signal and confirmed-helpful outcomes _before_ wiring any new signal into edge weights — same process that should have caught the current zeroUsage-beats-asIs regression earlier.

Related: AIBRAIN-67, AIBRAIN-31, AIBRAIN-71, AIBRAIN-62.

summary: Memory Trace panel in Obsidian plugin — expose retrieved/read/traversal lifecycle per query
description:
Extends the existing plugin (not the paused standalone desktop app, AIBRAIN-63) with a per-query trace view, so a human has something concrete to evaluate before we ask them "was this useful."

Show, per query, using data already logged by existing telemetry (AIBRAIN-71 event log):

* the query text
* notes retrieved (count + list)
* which of those were subsequently read
* whether a re-query on the same/similar topic followed (weak negative signal)

Example shape:

✓ authentication.md      READ
✓ oauth.md                READ

Explicitly do NOT attempt "used"/"referenced" attribution in this view — the plugin only surfaces what the server actually knows (see the evidence-state taxonomy story). No new instrumentation should be needed; this is a read/query layer over existing event logs.

Portability note: this is a consumer of the portable server-side event log, not a client-specific integration — any MCP client (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Gemini) can produce the underlying events this panel displays.

summary: Citation-token report_usage() experiment — measure real invocation rate
description:
Cheap experiment, explicitly not to be built into the ranking architecture until proven.

retrieve() returns each note with an opaque token (e.g. note A -> \[memory: m_123\]). Expose a tool, report_usage(tokens=\[...\]), described as expected-to-call after using retrieved context in an answer.

Known risk going in: this is structurally the same voluntary-compliance shape as reinforce_link, which had zero real invocations ever (see MCP Tool Decision-Delegation Audit) — an MCP server cannot force a client to call a second tool before ending its turn, on any client.

Deliverable is the measurement itself: implement cheaply, then track real invocation rate over a couple of weeks of live usage. If it's near-zero like reinforce_link, kill it and document that finding (useful negative result, not a failure) rather than iterating on it. If it's meaningfully non-zero, it becomes a "Referenced"-tier signal candidate alongside AIBRAIN-62's gateway work.

Related: AIBRAIN-71 (prior art on the same failure mode), AIBRAIN-62.

summary: search_notes returns empty for real notes — matching is literal substring only, no tokenization
description:
Found during a full-project audit (2026-09-02), reproduced live against the working vault (\~430 notes — NOT scale-dependent).

**Defect**: `searchNotes` (`packages/core/src/notes.ts`) matches with `title.toLowerCase().includes(needle)` / `aliases.some(a => a.includes(needle))` / `note.body.toLowerCase().includes(needle)`. The query is treated as one literal contiguous string. There is no tokenization, no OR/AND over terms, no stemming, no fuzzy fallback. Any query whose words are not a contiguous slice of the note returns `[]`.

**Reproduced**:

```
search_notes("MCP Tool Decision-Delegation Audit")
  -> 5 results (target found)

search_notes("decision delegation audit deterministic logging")
  -> []
```

The target note is `Notes/VaultNeuralLinks/MCP Tool Decision-Delegation Audit and Deterministic Logging Plan`. Every word of the second query appears in its title. It returns nothing.

**Why this matters more than it looks**: this is the actual root cause of the "search_notes returns empty for a confirmed-real note" symptom recorded twice in the vault (see the 2026-08-30 entry in `MOCs/VaultNeuralLinks` and the Related section of `Notes/VaultNeuralLinks/Usefulness Signal Roadmap - Pause Desktop UI, Sequence Evidence-State Telemetry`), which was tentatively attributed to AIBRAIN-132/133. Both of those tickets are about performance (crash and full-scan latency). Neither would fix this. It is also the worst failure mode available to an agent memory layer: the recall path reports confidently that nothing exists, and the calling LLM has no way to tell a real absence from a phrasing miss.

**Suggested fix**: tokenize the query, match on term overlap rather than substring containment, and score by term frequency / field weighting (see the sibling ranking bug for where the score should be applied). Should be designed alongside AIBRAIN-133's content index rather than after it, since the index format determines what matching is cheap.

Related: AIBRAIN-133 (content index — the same function, complementary fix), AIBRAIN-132 (crash fix in the same function).

summary: search_notes ranks by usage weight alone — exact title matches lose to incidental mentions in hub notes
description:
Found during a full-project audit (2026-09-02), reproduced live against the working vault.

**Defect**: after matching, `searchNotes` (`packages/core/src/notes.ts`) sorts with a single term:

```js
hits.sort((a, b) => (b.weight ?? 0) - (a.weight ?? 0));
```

`SearchHit.matched` ("title" | "alias" | "content") is computed, returned to the caller, and then discarded from ranking. There is no term-frequency score, no field weighting, no match-kind tier — nothing textual influences position at all. Usage weight is doing 100% of the ranking work.

**Reproduced** — `search_notes("MCP Tool Decision-Delegation Audit", topK: 5)`:

```
1  Notes/VaultNeuralLinks/Vault Neural Links Project        content  13.417
2  MOCs/VaultNeuralLinks                                    content  12.856
3  Notes/VaultNeuralLinks/Standalone Decoupled Product ...   content   5.531
4  Notes/VaultNeuralLinks/MCP Cross-Client Portability ...   content   0.150
5  Notes/VaultNeuralLinks/MCP Tool Decision-Delegation ...   title     0.150
```

The exact title match ranks **last**, behind two high-traffic hub notes that merely mention the phrase in passing. At the default `topK` of 10 it survives; at `topK: 4` it disappears entirely. Two notes tie at the 0.15 floor and their relative order is arbitrary.

**Why this is worth Highest priority**: this is the same pathology as AIBRAIN-130 (`asIs` 9/18 rank-1 vs `zeroUsage` 15/18), in a place where it takes one tool call to reproduce instead of a benchmark run. AIBRAIN-130 currently hypothesises stale/unpruned weights. This suggests a simpler and more general framing: **usage weight is being used as the ranking signal rather than as a tie-breaker on top of a relevance signal.** A note that is heavily traversed is heavily traversed for _everything_ — so on any query it outranks the note that actually answers it.

**Suggested fix**: score = relevance term (match kind tier: title > alias > content, plus term frequency once AIBRAIN-138 lands tokenization) with usage weight applied as a bounded multiplier or tie-breaker, not as the sort key. Then re-run `benchmark-baselines.mjs` / `benchmark-reinforcement.mjs` — if rank-1 on `asIs` moves toward `zeroUsage`, AIBRAIN-130 is substantially answered, and the same correction likely applies to `getWeightedNeighbors`/`activate`.

Related: AIBRAIN-130 (the inversion this is probably an instance of), AIBRAIN-138 (tokenization, same function), AIBRAIN-134 (evidence-state taxonomy — the "don't wire a signal into weights before measuring its correlation" principle this violates in the search path).

summary: Relevance-ranked plain-text search now beats activate() on rank-1 — re-examine whether the Hebbian/spreading-activation layer earns its complexity
description:
Side effect discovered while fixing AIBRAIN-138/139 (`bc508f5`), not something either of those tickets set out to find.

`benchmark-baselines.mjs`'s `grep` strategy is literally `searchNotes(vaultPath, label, { useWeights: false })` — no Hebbian weights, no spreading activation, no priming, no importance blending. Once AIBRAIN-138/139 gave it tokenized matching and match-kind-tiered ranking (title > alias > content, no usage signal at all since `useWeights:false`), re-running the same 18-query set:

| method | found | rank-1 | mean rank |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| grep (searchNotes, no weights) — before | 8/18 | 2/18 | 3.75 |
| grep (searchNotes, no weights) — after | 15/18 | **13/18** | 1.27 |
| engine (activate(), full mechanism stack) | 16/18 | 9/18 | 3.06 |
| structuralOnly (plain wikilink graph) | 9/18 | 1/18 | 14.67 |

Stable across two consecutive runs. The plain-text baseline — a function with none of the product's actual mechanism (decay, priming, consolidation, spreading activation, importance, Hebbian reinforcement) — now beats the full `activate()` engine on rank-1 accuracy, 13/18 vs 9/18.

**What this does and doesn't mean:**

* Does not resolve AIBRAIN-130 (the `asIs`-vs-`zeroUsage` inversion in `activate()`) — confirmed by re-running `benchmark-reinforcement.mjs` after this fix; those numbers are unchanged (`asIs` 9/18, `zeroUsage` 15/18), because `activate()`/`getWeightedNeighbors` is a different ranking path that AIBRAIN-138/139 didn't touch.
* It does sharpen the question AIBRAIN-130 already raised. Not just "is the usage tier calibrated correctly" but "does the whole activation/reinforcement machinery earn its cost over a much simpler baseline, once that baseline is given a fair basic implementation." Two bugs in a \~15-line naive-search function were apparently large enough to erase most of its measured disadvantage against the sophisticated engine.
* The 18-query set is small (n=18, one vault, one author writing both notes and ground truth) — this result should be treated as a strong lead, not a verdict, until AIBRAIN-130's honest-benchmark rebuild (real usage replayed from history predating the query set, no privileged event on the target) is in place. Same instrument caveat as AIBRAIN-130 itself.

**Suggested next step:** once AIBRAIN-130 is root-caused (or the same relevance-tier idea is tried in `getWeightedNeighbors`/`query.ts`, which currently sorts on weight alone with no query term at all since it's neighbor lookup, not search), re-run this comparison. If `activate()` still doesn't clear the fixed grep baseline by a meaningful margin, that's the answer to whether the reinforcement engine belongs at the center of the product's positioning, or whether structure + priming + importance (which already clearly beats grep pre-fix) is the sellable core and reinforcement is a smaller refinement on top.

Related: AIBRAIN-130 (the underlying inversion), AIBRAIN-138/AIBRAIN-139 (the fixes that produced this result), AIBRAIN-134 (evidence-state taxonomy — same "measure before you trust a signal" principle this result reinforces).

parentSummary: Retrieval Benchmark vs. Baselines + Personal Usage Analytics
summary: Priming has no intra-session decay — a note touched early in a long session stays top-tier after it stops being relevant
description:
Known gap, originally surfaced in AIBRAIN-30's literature review ("one real gap found: priming has no intra-session decay per ACT-R") but not acted on at the time since priming's flat `+2` bonus rarely won against real usage weight in practice.

That's no longer true after AIBRAIN-130's fix (`be88d9b`): a primed neighbor's weight is now floored above the strongest unprimed competitor in its neighbor set, specifically so priming reliably wins the comparison it's meant to win. That makes priming's dominance — and therefore its lack of recency-within-buffer decay (`primingBonus()` in `priming.ts`: "deliberately not weighted by recency-within-buffer") — matter more than it did before the fix.

Concretely: `SessionBuffer` is an LRU with no timestamp per entry. A note touched at the start of a long session stays exactly as "primed" as one touched a second ago, until it's evicted by the buffer filling up (default capacity 20). Under AIBRAIN-130's fix, that note now reliably outranks real usage-weighted hubs for as long as it stays in the buffer — including well after the session has moved on to a different topic.

Suggested approach: weight `primingBonus` (or the AIBRAIN-130 floor built on top of it) by recency-within-buffer instead of treating buffer membership as binary — e.g. a decay curve over buffer position, or an actual timestamp per touch. ACT-R's own activation-decay model (already the citation basis for `decay.ts`'s exponential decay) is the natural reference rather than inventing a new curve.

Not scoped further than this — needs its own design pass, not a quick tack-on to AIBRAIN-130.

parentSummary: searchNotes has no content index — full-vault linear scan takes 130s+ at 300k-note scale
summary: Content index doesn't narrow enough for corpora with heavily repeated vocabulary — candidates still need per-file reads
description:
Honest follow-up from AIBRAIN-133's real-scale validation, not a bug in what shipped.

**Measured** against sample-okf-large (300k notes, AIBRAIN-108's synthetic scale fixture): a query on terms that are common in this corpus's own vocabulary ("interface protocol context", each term present in \~125k/300k notes — this generator reuses a small, heavily-repeated word pool) narrows via token-intersection from 300,000 to 28,920 candidates in 57ms — the index and intersection logic themselves are fast. But 28,920 is still large enough that per-candidate disk reads (`readNote()` for anything the title-only fast path doesn't resolve) dominate again: 336s (no index) → 206s (indexed) — a real win, just a much smaller one than the 158x seen on a selective/zero-hit query (336s → 2.1s, same corpus).

**Root cause**: the index deliberately only answers "could this note possibly match" (AIBRAIN-133's design choice, to stay field-agnostic and always trust live content for scoring rather than risk a stale index producing a wrong tier/quality). For a corpus where common words are genuinely common, that candidate set doesn't shrink enough to avoid the read cost it was meant to eliminate.

**Not urgent**: the real `ai-brain` vault (471 notes, this repo's own) has genuinely diverse vocabulary (20,886 unique tokens across 471 notes) — nothing close to this synthetic corpus's \~1:1 token-to-note repetition ratio. This is a synthetic-fixture-specific stress case, not something observed against real usage.

**Possible direction, not decided**: have postings carry enough per-candidate information (e.g. which field it matched in, or a cheap term-frequency count) to let a common-case candidate be scored without a re-read at all. Deferred rather than attempted here because it reopens the exact staleness/consistency tradeoff AIBRAIN-133 deliberately avoided by keeping the index field-agnostic — needs its own design pass, not a quick tack-on.

Related: AIBRAIN-133 (the index this measures), AIBRAIN-108 (the scale fixture that surfaced it).
